title: Rayleigh-Wood Threshold Controls Nonlinear Photon Correlations in Atomic Arrays
abstract: Two-dimensional atomic arrays provide versatile free-space quantum optical interfaces by coupling photons to collective lattice modes. Here we show that the Rayleigh--Wood anomaly provides a sharp control mechanism for both linear and nonlinear photon scattering from a single atomic layer. As the lattice spacing crosses the diffraction threshold, newly opened radiative channels rapidly broaden the dominant collective modes, converting specular reflection into diffuse off-axis scattering. In transmission, momentum-space Fano interference between the incident and collectively scattered fields produces single-photon intensity zeros that strongly reshape the momentum-space correlation pattern. An integrated nonlinear contrast reveals a pronounced channel asymmetry: upon opening the Rayleigh channels, the connected two-photon contribution drops by several orders of magnitude relative to the factorized background in transmission, while remaining close to unity in reflection. These results establish radiative diffraction thresholds as a control principle for quantum nonlinear optics in single-layer atomic arrays.
summary: The authors demonstrate that the Rayleigh-Wood anomaly in 2D atomic arrays provides a powerful control mechanism for quantum nonlinear optics. By tuning the lattice spacing across the diffraction threshold, they show that the system can selectively suppress nonlinear correlations in transmitted light while preserving them in reflected light. This establishes diffraction thresholds as a general control principle for quantum nonlinear interactions in atomic structures.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the Rayleigh-Wood anomaly can be used to precisely control both linear and nonlinear photon scattering processes within single-layer atomic arrays.
main_result: The diffraction threshold acts as a sharp control knob, selectively collapsing the relative nonlinear two-photon correlation in transmitted light while leaving the reflected correlation largely unaffected.
method: The analysis uses input-output formalism and quantum regression theorem to calculate linear and two-photon scattering amplitudes, decomposing the nonlinear response into connected and factorized parts.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional atomic array modeled as a quantum metasurface, whose collective modes are governed by an effective Hamiltonian incorporating atom-photon interactions. The physics is analyzed across the transition point where the lattice spacing crosses the diffraction threshold.
key_observables: Specular reflection rate ($R_{	ext{spec}}$), transmission rate ($T_{	ext{spec}}$), two-photon scattering amplitude ($A^{(2)}$), and the integrated nonlinear contrast ($C_{\alpha\alpha}$).
important_parameters: Lattice spacing ($a$) relative to the resonant wavelength ($\lambda_0$), and the diffraction threshold ($a/\lambda_0 \approx 1$).
main_assumptions: The effective two-level description of the atoms is assumed to be valid, and the incident pulses are treated as quasi-monochromatic paraxial pulses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the abrupt drop of specular reflection and the development of diffuse scattering at the threshold, alongside plots showing the collapse of the connected two-photon contribution in transmission versus reflection across the anomaly.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the linear response (specular vs. diffuse scattering) first, establishing the physical mechanism of the Rayleigh-Wood anomaly, and then extends this analysis to the nonlinear regime by examining the connected two-photon correlations.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally tunable mechanism (diffraction threshold) to switch quantum nonlinear optical responses, which is highly relevant for designing quantum light sources and nonlinear quantum interfaces.
